1.title: Expositio litteralis capituli primi in Jonam prophetam: Et factum est verbum Domini ad Jonam, etc.
1.title_en: Literal exposition of the first chapter of the prophet Jonas: Now the word of the Lord came to Jonas, etc.

paras.t: Ipse Jonas, cui quæ subsequuntur contigerunt, eadem scripsit, et ait: Et factum est verbum Domini ad Jonam filium Amathi, dicens. In exordio ponit conjunctionem, Et, quæ poni consuevit in medio eorum quæ jungit. Sed idcirco nunc in principio ponitur, quoniam Jonas more prophetico multa in spiritu videns, et quod aliis Prophetis suo tempore et ante multa revelata essent cognoscens, his quæ vidit in spiritu, et quæ ab aliis visa fuerunt, conjungit quæ in isto descripsit volumine. Denique quod ait, Filium Amathi, secundum Hieronymum et Hebræos, ita exponitur, id est, filium veritatis: ita quod Amathi, est hic nomen commune seu appellativum, significans veritatem. Quum enim Elias defunctum puerum suscitasset, mater locuta est: Nunc in isto cognovi quia vir Dei es tu, et verbum Domini in ore tuo verum est. Ideo pro signo veritatis verborum divinorum in ore Eliæ, puer ille post suscitationem dictus est filius veritatis.
paras.en: Jonas himself, to whom the things that follow happened, wrote them down, and says: [[1:1|Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah, the son of Amathi, saying|Et factum est verbum Domini ad Jonam filium Amathi, dicens]]. At the beginning he puts the conjunction *And* [the Latin opens with *Et*, "And", which the Douay-Rheims renders "Now"], which is usually put between the things it joins. But it is put at the beginning here because Jonas, seeing many things in the spirit in the prophetic manner, and knowing that many things had been revealed to other Prophets in his own time and before, joins what he has written in this volume to the things he saw in the spirit and to those seen by others. Then, what he says, [[1:1|the son of Amathi|Filium Amathi]], is explained according to Jerome and the Hebrews thus: that is, *son of truth*; so that *Amathi* is here a common or appellative noun [that is, an ordinary word, not a proper name], meaning *truth*. For when Elias had raised the dead boy to life, his mother said: [[3 Kings 17:24|Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and the word of the Lord in thy mouth is true|Nunc in isto cognovi quia vir Dei es tu, et verbum Domini in ore tuo verum est]]. Therefore, as a sign of the truth of the divine words in the mouth of Elias, that boy after he was raised was called *son of truth*.

paras.t: Verumtamen aliqui dicunt, quod Amathi sit nomen proprium patris Jonæ. Quod quidam improbans, arguit: Mater Jonæ erat gentilis, quia de ea Christus loquitur apud Lucam: Multæ viduæ erant in diebus Eliæ in Israel; et ad nullam illarum missus est Elias, nisi in Sarepta Sidoniæ. Ergo et vir ejus fuit gentilis. Talibus autem non datur spiritus prophetiæ. Si autem Amathi est nomen patris Jonæ, oportet fateri quod erat propheta, quum regula sit Judæorum, quod omnes illi prophetæ fuerunt, qui in principio librorum prophetalium exprimuntur tanquam patres Prophetarum. — Sed quidquid sit de veritate conclusionis, argumentum istud non reputatur idoneum, et præmissæ ejus non carent errore. Non enim sequitur: mater fuit gentilis, ergo et pater. Personæ namque Hebrææ illo in tempore per mundum dispersæ, interdum cum gentilibus matrimonium contraxerunt. Unde et Lucas refert in Actibus Apostolorum: Timotheus filius erat mulieris fidelis (haud dubium quin Hebrææ), patre gentili. Idem patet de Hiram, quem rex Tyri misit ad Salomonem pro templi structura, ut scribitur tertio Regum. Quod autem gentilibus datus est spiritus prophetiæ, patet in Job viro sancto et vero propheta; et item in Balaam vero propheta, quamvis viro perverso. Prophetia namque est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, quæ virtuosis vitiosisque communis est.
paras.en: Some, however, say that *Amathi* is the proper name of Jonas's father. A certain writer, rejecting this, argues: Jonas's mother was a Gentile, since Christ speaks of her in Luke: [[Luke 4:25|there were many widows in the days of Elias in Israel|Multæ viduæ erant in diebus Eliæ in Israel]]; [[Luke 4:26|And to none of them was Elias sent, but to Sarepta of Sidon|et ad nullam illarum missus est Elias, nisi in Sarepta Sidoniæ]]. Therefore her husband too was a Gentile. But the spirit of prophecy is not given to such men. Yet if *Amathi* is the name of Jonas's father, we must grant that he was a prophet, since it is a rule of the Jews that all those were prophets who are named at the beginning of the prophetic books as the fathers of the Prophets. — But whatever be the truth of the conclusion, this argument is not thought sound, and its premisses are not free of error. For it does not follow: the mother was a Gentile, therefore the father was too. For Hebrew persons, scattered through the world at that time, sometimes contracted marriage with Gentiles. Hence Luke too relates in the Acts of the Apostles that Timothy was the son of a believing woman (no doubt a Hebrew), [[Acts 16:1|but his father was a Gentile|patre gentili]]. The same is plain of Hiram, whom the king of Tyre sent to Solomon for the building of the temple, as is written in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 7:13||]][[3 Kings 7:14||]] [there it is Solomon who sends for Hiram, the son of a widow of the tribe of Nephthali and of a Tyrian father; that the king of Tyre sent him is told in 2 Par 2:13]. And that the spirit of prophecy has been given to Gentiles is plain in Job, a holy man and a true prophet, and likewise in Balaam, a true prophet though a wicked man. For prophecy is a gift of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: a grace given for the good of others, not one that makes its bearer holy], which is common to the virtuous and the vicious.

paras.t: Surge, et vade in Niniven civitatem grandem: cujus magnitudo infra describitur, quoniam continebat iter trium dierum. Hanc Nemrod legitur ædificasse in Genesi. Et prædica in ea, quia ascendit malitia ejus coram me: id est, Ninivitis aperte denuntia, quod peccata eorum tam multa et magna sunt quod requirunt vindictam; et ipsi taliter prævaricantes, digni sunt obrui seu subverti, id est ab hostibus superari, vel aliunde plagari, seu divinitus destrui. Quemadmodum autem peccata dicuntur coram Deo clamare, ita dicuntur ascendere. Unde vox sanguinis Abel et peccata Sodomorum dicuntur clamare ad Dominum.
paras.en: [[1:2|Arise and go to Ninive, the great city|Surge, et vade in Niniven civitatem grandem]]: its size is described below, since it held a journey of three days[[Jon 3:3||]]. We read in Genesis that Nemrod built it[[Gen 10:8||]][[Gen 10:11||]] [the Douay-Rheims has "Out of that land came forth Assur, and built Ninive"; Denis follows the reading by which Nemrod went out of that land into Assur and built Ninive]. [[1:2|and preach in it: For the wickedness thereof is come up before me|Et prædica in ea, quia ascendit malitia ejus coram me]]: that is, openly declare to the Ninivites that their sins are so many and so great that they call for vengeance; and that they, transgressing in this way, deserve to be overwhelmed or overthrown: that is, to be overcome by enemies, or stricken in some other way, or destroyed by God. And just as sins are said to cry out before God, so they are said to go up. Hence the voice of the blood of Abel[[Gen 4:10||]] and the sins of the Sodomites[[Gen 18:20||]][[Gen 19:13||]] are said to cry to the Lord.

paras.t: Et surrexit Jonas, ut fugeret in Tharsis, id est in Tarsum urbem Ciliciæ, secundum Josephum et alios multos. De qua civitate fuit Paulus, de quo in Actibus Apostolorum dicitur: Quære Saulum nomine Tarsensem. Judæi autem nomine Tharsis intelligunt generaliter mare. Quod secundum Hieronymum huic loco amplius congruit, scilicet, ut fugitivus et timidus non in certum locum, sed quocumque eum mare deferret, intelligatur fugisse. Quidam nihilo minus per Tharsis intelligunt urbem Indiæ. A facie Domini, id est a præsentia seu jussione divina, quasi locum mutando, posset conspectum seu potestatem Dei effugere, æstimans quod iram Dei vitare posset in alieno loco, scilicet, si Judæam relinquat, in qua solummodo Deum notum putavit. Sed mirum videtur, si vir sanctus, qui non solum revelationes in hoc libro descriptas sortitus est, sed etiam, sicut nunc tactum est, de regno Israel prophetavit, adeo simplex fuit, quod nescivit Deum esse ubique per essentiam et omnipotentiam, nec manum ejus quemquam effugere posse: quod in Scripturis veteris Testamenti tam ubertim habetur, ut quum ait Psalmista: Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam? et, Quia in manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ; et, Domini est terra et plenitudo ejus. Ad quod dicendum opinor, quod utique novit Deum ubique præsentem et æque potentem, sed fugit ut Deus haberet eum de injuncto obsequio supportatum, dum cerneret eum tam invite exsequi quod sibi impositum fuit. Vel forte putavit quod propter inobedientiam suam tolleretur ab eo spiritus prophetiæ. Aliqui autem affirmant, quod fugit quia pro tunc non fiebant revelationes propheticæ, nisi in terra duodecim tribuum Israel: quod modice valet, præsertim quum Eliæ factæ sint multæ revelationes in monte […]bens ut iret ad Pharaonem et filios Israel, satis frequenter et diu se excusavit. Sic potest opinari de Jona, qui tamen non excusatur in toto.
paras.en: [[1:3|And Jonah rose up to flee into Tharsis|Et surrexit Jonas, ut fugeret in Tharsis]]: that is, to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, according to Josephus and many others. Paul was of that city, of whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 9:11|seek|Quære]] [[Acts 9:11|one named Saul of Tarsus|Saulum nomine Tarsensem]]. But the Jews understand by the name *Tharsis* the sea in general. According to Jerome this fits the passage better: namely, that he is to be understood to have fled, a fugitive and afraid, not to a set place, but wherever the sea might carry him. Some, nevertheless, understand by *Tharsis* a city of India. [[1:3|from the face of the Lord|A facie Domini]], that is, from the divine presence or command, as though by changing place he could escape the sight or the power of God, thinking that he could avoid God's anger in a foreign place, namely if he left Judea, in which alone he thought God was known. But it seems strange that a holy man, who not only received the revelations described in this book but also, as has just been touched on, prophesied about the kingdom of Israel [see 4 Kings 14:25], should have been so simple as not to know that God is everywhere by His essence and omnipotence, and that no one can escape His hand: a thing found so abundantly in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, as when the Psalmist says: [[Ps 138:7|Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face?|Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam?]] and, [[Ps 94:4|For in his hand are all the ends of the earth|Quia in manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ]]; and, [[Ps 23:1|The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof|Domini est terra et plenitudo ejus]]. To this I think it must be said that he certainly knew God to be present everywhere and equally powerful, but he fled so that God might hold him excused from the service enjoined, on seeing him carry out so unwillingly what had been laid upon him. Or perhaps he thought that because of his disobedience the spirit of prophecy would be taken from him. Some, however, maintain that he fled because at that time prophetic revelations were made only in the land of the twelve tribes of Israel: which carries little weight, especially since many revelations were made to Elias on the mount […] that he should go to Pharao and the children of Israel, excused himself often enough and at length[[Ex 3:1||]][[Ex 4:1||]]. So one may think of Jonas, who nevertheless is not wholly excused.

paras.t: Et descendit in Joppen, id est urbem sic dictam. Venit enim ad portum civitatis illius, in qua est portus Judææ, ubi intratur ad Mediterraneum mare. Terra quoque de qua venit Jonas, fuit altior situ quam Joppe: ideo pergendo Joppen, scribitur descendisse. Et invenit navem euntem in Tharsis, id est in mare, vel civitatem sic dictam, ut habitum est; et dedit magistro navis naulum ejus, id est pretium pro sua deportatione in navi, et descendit in eam, ut iret, id est navigaret, cum eis qui erant in navi, in Tharsis a facie Domini, ut cessaret alloqui fugientem de causa propter quam fugit. Verumtamen Dominus non sine multiplici ratione permisit Prophetam suum sic fugere, ut patebit.
paras.en: [[1:3|and he went down to Joppe|Et descendit in Joppen]], that is, to the city so called. For he came to the harbour of that city, in which is the port of Judea, where one enters the Mediterranean Sea. Also, the land from which Jonas came lay higher than Joppe: therefore, in going to Joppe, he is written to have gone down. [[1:3|and found a ship going to Tharsis|Et invenit navem euntem in Tharsis]], that is, to the sea, or to the city so called, as has been said; [[1:3|and he paid|et dedit]] the master of the ship [[1:3|the fare thereof|naulum ejus]], that is, the price for his carriage in the ship, [[1:3|and went down into it, to go|et descendit in eam, ut iret]], that is, to sail, [[1:3|with them|cum eis]] who were in the ship, [[1:3|to Tharsis from the face of the Lord|in Tharsis a facie Domini]], so that He might cease to speak to him, fleeing, about the matter for which he fled. Yet the Lord, not without manifold reason, allowed His Prophet to flee in this way, as will appear.

paras.t: Dominus autem misit ventum magnum in mare, supernaturaliter concitando hanc commotionem ac tempestatem. Et facta est tempestas magna in mari, ita quod undæ aquarum omniquaque exsurgebant circa hanc navem repente ac vehementer, et navis periclitabatur conteri, id est, periculum destructionis et submersionis imminebat propter concussionem aquarum ad navem, quæ fluctibus terribiliter jactabatur.
paras.en: [[1:4|But the Lord sent a great wind to the sea|Dominus autem misit ventum magnum in mare]], stirring up this commotion and storm supernaturally. [[1:4|and a great tempest was raised in the sea|Et facta est tempestas magna in mari]], so that the waves of the waters rose up on every side about this ship suddenly and violently, [[1:4|and the ship was in danger to be broken|et navis periclitabatur conteri]]: that is, the danger of destruction and sinking hung over it because of the battering of the waters against the ship, which was tossed terribly by the billows.

paras.t: Et nautæ timuerunt instans periculum, et clamaverunt viri ad deum suum. Dicunt aliqui, quod in navi erant homines diversorum territoriorum ac rituum, diversos deos colentium, sicque unusquisque suum invocavit deum. Huic dicto consonat translatio Septuaginta interpretum, quæ talis est: Et clamaverunt unusquisque ad deum suum. Quamvis enim veritatem Dei summi ignorarent, credebant tamen esse providentiam, et mundum inferiorem gubernari a diis, quorum auxilio æstimabant mare posse sedari. Sicque sub errore religionis noverant aliquid venerandum. Et miserunt vasa quæ erant in navi, in mare, ut alleviaretur navis ab eis, ut scilicet pondere vasorum ejecto, navis facilius transiliret, quam arbitrabantur solito onere prægravari.
paras.en: [[1:5|And the mariners were afraid|Et nautæ timuerunt]] of the danger at hand, [[1:5|and the men cried to their god|et clamaverunt viri ad deum suum]]. Some say that in the ship there were men of different lands and rites, worshipping different gods, and so each called upon his own god. With this saying agrees the translation of the Seventy interpreters, which runs thus: *And they cried, each one to his god.* For although they did not know the truth of the supreme God, they believed nevertheless that there is a providence, and that the lower world is governed by gods, by whose help they thought the sea could be calmed. And so, under an error of religion, they knew of something to be worshipped. [[1:5|and they cast forth the wares that were in the ship, into the sea, to lighten it|Et miserunt vasa quæ erant in navi, in mare, ut alleviaretur]], the ship, [[1:5|of them|ab eis]]: so that, the weight of the wares being thrown out, the ship, which they thought weighed down by its usual load, might ride the waves more easily.

paras.t: Et Jonas descendit ad interiora navis, id est ad secretiora ejus latibula, et dormiebat sopore gravi, id est dure seu fortiter. Cur ad interiora navis ingressus est atque dormivit? Dici potest, quod videns tempestatem oriri, et de peccato fugæ conscius sibi, agnovit eam propter se concitari: ideo jam mœstus ac pavens, et instans malum intueri non audens, intravit latibulum, et præ tristitia tædioque dormivit, sicut Apostoli tempore passionis. Et Psalmista: Dormitavit, inquit, anima mea præ tædio. Alii dicunt, quod in tanta tempestate tranquillus fuit atque securus, aliisque turbatis placido somno quievit. Sed mirum apparet, si tempestatem videns insurgere, et agnoscens eam propter suam culpam accidere, non potius dedit se ad orandum corde timorato atque sollicito somnum excludente, quam ad dormiendum: maxime, ne occasione ipsius omnes perirent qui erant in navi. Potius igitur reor, quod statim postquam navis ingressa est mare, tempestate nondum exorta, Jonas ad interiora navis descendit, tanquam lassus de via, et tristis propter commissionem sibi factam. Et quia cum illis gentilibus non delectabatur misceri, idcirco dedit se repausationi soporis. Somnus enim naturaliter mitigat cordis tristitiam.
paras.en: [[1:5|and Jonah went down into the inner part of the ship|Et Jonas descendit ad interiora navis]], that is, to its more hidden recesses, [[1:5|and fell into a deep sleep|et dormiebat sopore gravi]], that is, heavily or soundly. Why did he go into the inner part of the ship and sleep? It can be said that, seeing the storm arise, and conscious of the sin of his flight, he recognized that it was raised up on his account: therefore, now sad and fearful, and not daring to look upon the evil at hand, he went into a hiding-place, and slept for sorrow and weariness, as the Apostles did at the time of the Passion[[Matt 26:40||]][[Matt 26:43||]]. And the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:28|My soul hath slumbered|Dormitavit]], [[Ps 118:28|through heaviness|anima mea præ tædio]] [Denis's word order is *Dormitavit, inquit, anima mea præ tædio*: "My soul slumbered, he says, through weariness"]. Others say that in so great a storm he was calm and untroubled, and while the others were in turmoil he rested in peaceful sleep. But it seems strange that, seeing the storm rise and recognizing that it came about through his own fault, he did not rather give himself to prayer, with a fearful and anxious heart that would shut out sleep, than to sleeping: above all lest all who were in the ship should perish on his account. I think, therefore, rather that immediately after the ship had put to sea, before the storm had arisen, Jonas went down into the inner part of the ship, as one weary from the journey and sad because of the charge laid upon him. And because he took no pleasure in mixing with those Gentiles, he therefore gave himself to the rest of sleep. For sleep naturally soothes the sorrow of the heart.

paras.t: Et accessit ad eum gubernator, id est rector navis, qui tanquam superior alios habuit consolari, et de remedio principaliter sollicitari, et dixit ei: Quid tu sopore deprimeris? id est, cur tantæ temeritatis atque ignaviæ es, ut in tanto discrimine dormias? Surge, invoca Deum tuum, ut cujus commune exstat periculum, sit et communis oratio. Vidit enim gubernator quod vasa jactando et idola implorando nihil proficerent: idcirco alloquitur Jonam, quem vidit hucusque non exorasse, præsertim quum naturale sit, unumquemque in suo periculo plus de alio quam in se ipso confidere. Si forte recogitet Deus tuus de nobis, quibus nostri dii non auxiliantur, id est, quatenus Deus tuus subveniendo ostendat se memoriam nostri, quorum videtur oblitus, ut non pereamus, id est, ne mergamur.
paras.en: [[1:6|And the ship master came to him|Et accessit ad eum gubernator]], that is, the master of the ship, who as the one in charge had to comfort the others and be chiefly concerned about a remedy, [[1:6|and said to him: Why art thou fast asleep|et dixit ei: Quid tu sopore deprimeris]]? that is, why are you so rash and so slothful as to sleep in so great a peril? [[1:6|rise up call upon thy God|Surge, invoca Deum tuum]], so that where the danger is common, the prayer may be common too. For the master saw that they gained nothing by throwing out the wares and imploring idols: therefore he speaks to Jonas, whom he saw had not prayed till then, especially since it is natural for each man in his danger to trust more in another than in himself. [[1:6|if so be that God will think of us|Si forte recogitet Deus tuus de nobis]], whom our gods do not help: that is, so that thy God, by coming to our aid, may show that He is mindful of us, whom He seems to have forgotten, [[1:6|that we may not perish|ut non pereamus]], that is, that we may not be sunk.

paras.t: Et dixit vir ad collegam suum, id est, viri isti inter se loquebantur. Non dubium quin Jonas surgens invocaverit Deum, sed quum nec ejus oratio præberet subsidium, dixerunt quod subditur: Venite, mittamus sortes, et sciamus quare hoc malum pœnale, id est ista afflictio, sit nobis. Nautæ et viri isti naturam ventorum ac tempestatum frequenter experti, pensabant tempestatem hanc non esse naturalem ac solitam, sed propter alicujus in navi consistentis maleficium contigisse. Aliter non sorte quærerent auctorem naufragii, nec per rem incertam, certum periculum conarentur vitare. Et miserunt sortes, et cecidit sors super Jonam. Sortes enim mittuntur in sinum, sed a Domino temperantur, ut dicitur in Proverbiorum libro.
paras.en: [[1:7|And they said every one to his fellow|Et dixit vir ad collegam suum]]: that is, these men spoke among themselves. No doubt Jonas got up and called upon God; but since not even his prayer brought help, they said what follows: [[1:7|Come and let us cast lots, that we may know why this evil|Venite, mittamus sortes, et sciamus quare hoc malum]] (an evil of punishment, that is, this affliction) [[1:7|is upon us|sit nobis]]. These sailors and men, often acquainted by experience with the nature of winds and storms, judged that this storm was not natural and usual, but had come about through the wrongdoing of someone in the ship. Otherwise they would not have sought by lot the cause of the shipwreck, nor tried to avoid a certain danger by an uncertain means. [[1:7|And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah|Et miserunt sortes, et cecidit sors super Jonam]]. For [[Prov 16:33|Lots are cast into the lap, but they are disposed of by the Lord|Sortes enim mittuntur in sinum, sed a Domino temperantur]], as is said in the book of Proverbs.

paras.t: Quæritur, an liceat sortibus uti. Videtur quod imo, auctoritate Salomonis nunc posita. Josue quoque per sortem deprehendit Achan. Apostoli etiam usi sunt sorte in electione Matthiæ. Præterea Moyses ait in Numerorum libro, ut terra promissionis per sortes divideretur: Sicut, inquit, unicuique sors ceciderit, tribuetur hereditas. Oppositum autem arguitur, quoniam Glossa ait hoc loco (estque Glossa hæc sumpta ex verbis Hieronymi): Quod Matthias sorte eligitur, et hic fugitivus, scilicet Jonas, sorte deprehenditur, non agitur virtute sortium, sed voluntate Dei, qui sortes regebat incertas. Nec hoc exemplo debemus uti vel credere sortibus, quoniam privilegia singulorum non possunt legem facere communem: sicut nec ubique credendum est somniis, quamvis voluntate Dei Pharao et Nabuchodonosor indicio somniorum futura cognoscunt, videlicet per interpretationem Joseph et Danielis.
paras.en: It is asked whether it is lawful to use lots. It seems that it is, by the authority of Solomon just set down. Josue, too, found out Achan by lot[[Jos 7:14||]][[Jos 7:16||]][[Jos 7:18||]]. The Apostles also used the lot in the election of Matthias[[Acts 1:26||]]. Moreover, Moses says in the book of Numbers that the land of promise should be divided by lots: [[Num 33:54|To every one as the lot shall fall, so shall the inheritance be given|unicuique sors ceciderit, tribuetur hereditas]], he says. Against this it is argued that the Gloss says on this place (and this Gloss is taken from the words of Jerome): *That Matthias is chosen by lot, and that this fugitive, namely Jonas, is found out by lot, is not brought about by the power of lots but by the will of God, who governed the uncertain lots. Nor ought we by this example to use or trust in lots, since the privileges of individuals cannot make a common law; just as dreams are not to be trusted everywhere, although by the will of God Pharao and Nabuchodonosor came to know the future by the sign of dreams*[[Gen 41:1||]][[Dan 2:1||]][[Dan 4:1||]], namely through the interpretation of Joseph and of Daniel.

paras.t: Et respondendum secundum Thomam in secunda secundæ, quod sortes dicuntur, dum aliqua fiunt, ex quorum eventu aliquid occultum innotescit. Triplex ergo est sors, scilicet divisoria, consultoria, ac divinatoria. Divisoria appellatur, quia permissionem seu indicium sortium quæritur quid sit alicui exhibendum de re possessa, dignitate, honore vel pœna, hoc est, ut cognoscatur quis quam partem accipiat. Si autem quæritur quid sit agendum vel dimittendum, vocatur sors consultoria. Quod si investigetur quid sit futurum, erit sors divinatoria. Actus autem humani qui requiruntur ad sortes, non sunt subjecti influxioni stellarum. Non ergo licet effectum seu ostensionem sortium exspectare a corpore cœlesti seu astris, nec a spirituali substantia mala, scilicet dæmone. His autem causis remotis, oportet sortialium actuum effectum præstolari a fortuna, vel ex substantia spirituali directiva bona, puta a Deo vel angelis. Si itaque exspectetur a fortuna: quod in sorte divisoria tantummodo locum habet, ut dum aliqui nequeunt rem concorditer dividere, sorte utuntur, totum committentes fortunæ; tunc (ut aliqui dicunt) nullum est peccatum. Alii tamen asserunt quod sit vitium vanitatis. Porro si effectus sortis exspectetur a Deo vel ab angelis, non est in se malum, secundum Augustinum. Sed potest in hoc quadrupliciter peccatum incidere. Primo, si fiat sine necessitate, quia hoc pertinet ad tentationem Dei. Secundo, si etiam in necessitate fiat sine debita reverentia. Unde Apostoli cœtu fratrum collecto, et oratione præmissa, sortes miserunt. Tertio, si divina oracula ad terrena convertantur negotia. Quarto, si in ecclesiasticis electionibus, quæ ex Spiritus Sancti inspiratione fieri debent, sortibus quis utatur. Unde Beda dicit, Matthiam sorte electum seu factum apostolum, quando Spiritus Sanctus nondum erat datus; sed Spiritu Sancto recepto, septem diaconi non sorte sed fratrum electione sunt ordinati.
paras.en: And the answer must be, according to Thomas in the *Secunda Secundæ*, that lots are spoken of when certain things are done from whose outcome something hidden becomes known. The lot, then, is threefold: namely the dividing lot, the consulting lot and the divining lot. It is called *dividing* when by the casting or the indication of lots [the Latin has *permissionem*, apparently for *per missionem*, "by the casting"] it is sought what is to be given to someone of a possession, a dignity, an honour or a penalty; that is, so that it may be known who is to receive which part. But if it is sought what is to be done or left undone, it is called the *consulting* lot. And if what is to come is being searched out, it will be the *divining* lot. Now the human acts that lots require are not subject to the influence of the stars. It is therefore not lawful to look for the effect or the showing of lots from a heavenly body or the stars, nor from an evil spiritual substance, that is, a demon. These causes being set aside, the effect of the acts of casting lots must be awaited either from chance, or from a good directing spiritual substance, such as God or the angels. If, then, it is looked for from chance (which has place only in the dividing lot, as when some cannot divide a thing in agreement and use the lot, committing the whole to chance), then, as some say, there is no sin. Others, however, assert that it is the vice of vanity. Further, if the effect of the lot is looked for from God or from the angels, it is not evil in itself, according to Augustine. But sin can come into it in four ways. First, if it is done without necessity, for this belongs to tempting God. Second, if, even in necessity, it is done without due reverence. Hence the Apostles cast lots after gathering the company of the brethren and first praying. Third, if divine oracles are turned to earthly business. Fourth, if someone uses lots in ecclesiastical elections, which ought to be made by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost. Hence Bede says that Matthias was chosen or made an apostle by lot when the Holy Ghost had not yet been given; but once the Holy Ghost had been received, the seven deacons were ordained not by lot but by the election of the brethren.

paras.t: Ex quibus patet ad argumenta responsio. Verumtamen isti existentes in navi cum Jona, fuerunt gentiles, ideo superstitiosis sortibus usi creduntur. Unde nec excusantur in toto. Deus tamen qui de malis elicit bona, taliter temperavit has sortes, quod Jonas est deprehensus.
paras.en: From this the answer to the arguments is plain. Those who were in the ship with Jonas, however, were Gentiles, and so are believed to have used superstitious lots. Hence they are not wholly excused either. Yet God, who draws good out of evil, so disposed these lots that Jonas was found out.

paras.t: Et dixerunt ad eum: Indica nobis cujus causa, id est pro quo peccato, malum istud pœnæ, puta tempestas, sit nobis omnibus propter te solum. Deprehensum per sortem, cogunt propria voce confiteri quod verum est, ut certiores reddantur. Et forte specialiter mirabantur quod sors cecidit super Jonam, qui ex vultu et habitu, verbis et gestibus, videbatur homo virtutis. Ideo sciscitantur: Quod est opus tuum? id est, quid habes præ manibus? quid fecisti? cujus officii es? Primo quærunt de opere, quoniam propter opus efficitur homo dignus pœna vel laude. Quæ terra tua? id est, de qua regione es oriundus? et quo vadis? vel ex quo populo es tu, id est, cujus religionis et cultus? Quatuor ergo mira brevitate interrogant, ut ex his cognoscatur causa periculi. Aliquando enim quis punitur, propter malitiam terræ natalis, vel quia tendit ad locum prohibitum, vel propter peccata parentum.
paras.en: [[1:8|And they said to him: Tell us for what cause|Et dixerunt ad eum: Indica nobis cujus causa]], that is, for what sin, [[1:8|this evil|malum istud]] of punishment, namely the storm, [[1:8|is upon us|sit nobis]] all, on account of you alone. Him whom they had found out by lot they compel to confess with his own voice what is true, so that they may be made more certain. And perhaps they wondered especially that the lot fell upon Jonas, who by his face and bearing, his words and gestures, seemed a man of virtue. Therefore they ask: [[1:8|what is thy business|Quod est opus tuum]]? that is, what have you in hand? what have you done? what is your calling? They ask first about his work, since it is by his work that a man is made worthy of punishment or praise. [[1:8|of what country art thou|Quæ terra tua]]? that is, from what region do you come? [[1:8|and whither goest thou? or of what people art thou?|et quo vadis? vel ex quo populo es tu]], that is, of what religion and worship? So they ask four things with wonderful brevity, so that from them the cause of the danger may be known. For sometimes a man is punished for the wickedness of his native land, or because he is making for a forbidden place, or for the sins of his parents.

paras.t: Quibus Jonas plane breviterque respondet: Et dixit ad eos: Hebræus ego sum. Descendentes enim de genere Abrahæ per Isaac et Jacob, vocantur Hebræi ab Heber, de cujus semine natus est Abraham. Et Dominum Deum cœli ego timeo, id est, colo et vereor. Quum enim Jonas hæc dixit, timuit utique Deum, et de suo peccato (ut reor) pœnituit. Si vero dicatur peccasse mortaliter, fugiendo et non obediendo, amisit filialem timorem, quem pœnitendo recuperavit. Qui fecit mare et aridam: de quo in Apocalypsi legitur: Adorate eum qui fecit cœlum et terram, mare et fontes aquarum.
paras.en: Jonas answers them plainly and briefly: [[1:9|And he said to them: I am a Hebrew|Et dixit ad eos: Hebræus ego sum]]. For those descended from the race of Abraham through Isaac and Jacob are called Hebrews from Heber, of whose seed Abraham was born[[Gen 11:14||]][[Gen 11:26||]] [the margin gives Gen. xi, 14–26]. [[1:9|and I fear the Lord, and the God of heaven|Et Dominum Deum cœli ego timeo]], that is, I worship and revere Him. For when Jonas said this, he certainly feared God, and (as I think) repented of his sin. And if he is said to have sinned mortally by fleeing and not obeying, he lost filial fear, which he recovered by repenting. [[1:9|who made both the sea and the dry land|Qui fecit mare et aridam]]: of whom we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 14:7|adore ye him that made heaven and earth, the sea and the fountains of waters|Adorate eum qui fecit cœlum et terram, mare et fontes aquarum]].

paras.t: Et timuerunt viri timore magno: tamen servili. Timuerunt enim majestatem Creatoris, cujus omnipotentiam visibiliter sentiebant; et viderant quam horrendum esset manum illius incidere. Et dixerunt ad eum: Quid hoc fecisti? Quod intelligi potest dupliciter: Primo increpatorie, tanquam dicant: Cur tanto Deo non paruisti? et cur Creatoris manum putasti effugere? Secundo interrogative, ut sit sensus: Quod est mysterium fugæ tuæ? Cur vir tantus, tam religiosus et divinarum revelationum conscius fugit, nec studuit ire in Niniven ad prædicendum ejus subversionem? Cur cultor unius summi Dei recessit a Deo suo? Cognoverunt enim viri quod a facie Domini fugeret, quia indicaverat eis, quando dixit, Hebræus ego sum: tunc enim adjecit, quod fugeret a facie Domini, et idcirco oriretur tempestas.
paras.en: [[1:10|And the men were greatly afraid|Et timuerunt viri timore magno]]: yet with a servile fear [that is, fear of punishment, as distinct from the filial fear of offending God]. For they feared the majesty of the Creator, whose omnipotence they felt visibly; and they had seen how fearful a thing it was to fall into His hand[[Heb 10:31||]]. [[1:10|and they said to him: Why hast thou done this?|Et dixerunt ad eum: Quid hoc fecisti]] This can be understood in two ways. First, as a rebuke, as though they said: Why did you not obey so great a God? and why did you think to escape the Creator's hand? Second, as a question, so that the sense is: What is the mystery of your flight? Why has so great a man, so devout and acquainted with divine revelations, fled, and not taken care to go to Ninive to foretell its overthrow? Why has a worshipper of the one supreme God gone away from his God? [[1:10|For the men knew that he fled from the face of the Lord: because he had told them|Cognoverunt enim viri quod a facie Domini fugeret, quia indicaverat eis]], when he said, *I am a Hebrew*: for then he added that he was fleeing from the face of the Lord, and that this was why the storm had arisen.

paras.t: Et dixerunt ad eum: Quid faciemus tibi, et cessabit mare, id est commotio maris, a nobis? tanquam dicant: Videmus te virum esse magnum, sapientem et sanctum, cum quo loquitur Deus, cui sua secreta revelat, cui magna committit: ideo tibi cuncta committimus, et ut tui ipsius judex consistas. Tuum est imperare, nostrumque exsequi; et qui auctor es culpæ, demonstra remedium. Non audemus cultorem summi Dei proprio condemnare consilio, ne Dei ejus iram gravius incurramus. Quia mare ibat et intumescebat.
paras.en: [[1:11|And they said to him: What shall we do with thee, that the sea may be calm|Et dixerunt ad eum: Quid faciemus tibi, et cessabit mare]], that is, the commotion of the sea, [[1:11|to us|a nobis]]? as though they said: We see that you are a great man, wise and holy, with whom God speaks, to whom He reveals His secrets, to whom He entrusts great things: therefore we entrust everything to you, even that you be judge of yourself. It is for you to command, and for us to carry it out; and you who are the author of the fault, show the remedy. We dare not condemn a worshipper of the supreme God by our own decision, lest we incur his God's anger more heavily. [[1:11|for the sea flowed and swelled|Quia mare ibat et intumescebat]].

paras.t: Et dixit ad eos: Tollite me, et mittite in mare. In quo patet constantia et justitia Jonæ, qui contra se ipsum tam promptum pronuntiavit judicium, maluitque submergi, quam alios secum periclitari, paratus etiam mortem tolerare pro suo peccato, ad satisfaciendum honori divino. Et cessabit mare a vobis, quum fuero mersus. Culpa enim ulta, pœna finitur. Scio enim quod propter me tempestas hæc grandis est super vos, id est, idcirco condoleo vobis, et opto vos erui, me pereunte.
paras.en: [[1:12|And he said to them: take me up, and cast me into the sea|Et dixit ad eos: Tollite me, et mittite in mare]]. In this the constancy and justice of Jonas is plain, who pronounced so ready a sentence against himself, and chose rather to be drowned than that others should be in danger with him, ready even to suffer death for his sin, to make satisfaction to the divine honour. [[1:12|and the sea shall be calm to you|Et cessabit mare a vobis]], when I have been sunk. For when the fault is avenged, the punishment ends. [[1:12|for I know for my sake this great tempest is upon you|Scio enim quod propter me tempestas hæc grandis est super vos]]: that is, therefore I grieve with you, and wish you to be delivered, though I perish.

paras.t: Et remigaverunt viri, ut reverterentur ad aridam. In quo patet, quam invitissime ejecerunt Jonam propter reverentiam personæ, cui cum proprio periculo deferebant. Et non valebant reverti ad terram, quia mare ibat, id est, impetuose ferebatur, et intumescebat super eos, quasi non potens ultionem injuriæ sui Creatoris differre. Et quo viri illi plus tardabant submergere Jonam, eo altius irruit super eos fluctuum impetus. Dicunt quoque Hebræorum doctores nonnulli, quod aliæ naves vicinæ sine tempestatis concussione procedebant, sed huic navi ex omni latere imminebat tempestas, ita quod nec reverti valebant.
paras.en: [[1:13|And the men rowed hard to return the land|Et remigaverunt viri, ut reverterentur ad aridam]]. In this it is plain how very unwillingly they cast Jonas out, out of reverence for his person, to which they deferred at their own peril. [[1:13|but they were not able|Et non valebant]] to get back to land, [[1:13|because the sea tossed|quia mare ibat]], that is, was driven violently, [[1:13|and swelled upon them|et intumescebat super eos]], as though it could not put off avenging the wrong done to its Creator. And the longer those men delayed to sink Jonas, the higher the onrush of the waves broke over them. Some doctors of the Hebrews also say that other ships nearby went on without being battered by the storm, but that the storm beset this ship on every side, so that they could not get back.

paras.t: Et clamaverunt ad Dominum: jam enim ex effectu noverant causam, videlicet quod esset unus omnium Dominator summus atque omnipotens, cujus tantam experiebantur in mari virtutem; et dixerunt: Quæsumus, Domine, ne pereamus in anima viri istius, id est, ne ob interfectionem cultoris tui puniamur a te, et ne des super nos sanguinem innocentem, id est, nobis non imputetur mors Prophetæ sancti innoxii. Non quod fuerit penitus innocens, imo hanc meruit pœnam; sed aliunde erat vir sanctus et innocens, et cognoverunt eum esse meliorem eis: ideo metuebant manus peccatrices in vatem extendere. Quia tu, Domine, sicut voluisti, fecisti.
paras.en: [[1:14|And they cried to the Lord|Et clamaverunt ad Dominum]]: for now they knew the cause from the effect, namely that there was one supreme and almighty Ruler of all, whose great power they were experiencing on the sea; [[1:14|and said: We beseech thee, O Lord let us not perish for this man's life|et dixerunt: Quæsumus, Domine, ne pereamus in anima viri istius]], that is, let us not be punished by Thee for killing Thy worshipper, [[1:14|and lay not upon us innocent blood|et ne des super nos sanguinem innocentem]], that is, let not the death of a holy and guiltless Prophet be imputed to us. Not that he was wholly innocent; indeed he deserved this punishment; but otherwise he was a holy and innocent man, and they knew him to be better than themselves: therefore they feared to stretch out sinful hands against the prophet. [[1:14|for thou, oh Lord, hast done as it pleased thee|Quia tu, Domine, sicut voluisti, fecisti]].

paras.t: Et tulerunt Jonam, id est, spontaneum cum reverentia et timore portabant, non renitentem rapuerunt, et miserunt in mare; et stetit, id est, cessavit et conquievit, mare a fervore suo, id est impetuosa commotione simili iræ atque furoris.
paras.en: [[1:15|And they took Jonah|Et tulerunt Jonam]]: that is, they carried him, willing, with reverence and fear; they did not seize him struggling; [[1:15|and cast him into the sea|et miserunt in mare]]; [[1:15|and the sea ceased|et stetit]], that is, stopped and grew calm, [[1:15|from raging|mare a fervore suo]], that is, from its violent commotion, like anger and fury.

paras.t: Et timuerunt viri timore magno Dominum. Naturale est enim, ut insolitis ac mirabilibus rebus visis, homo formidet. Unde in Evangelio frequenter habetur, quod turbæ visis miraculis Christi, timuerunt. Viri autem prædicti multa mirabilia sub una hora viderunt, videlicet supernaturalis tempestatis ortum, et ejusdem subitaneam cessationem. Et immolaverunt hostias Domino, vel hostias laudis et spiritum contribulatum ac precem devotam, vel etiam hostias corporales de rebus suis quas secum habebant, et voverunt vota, id est, plura se oblaturos promiserunt. Imo, secundum Hieronymum, voverunt se amplius non recessuros a Deo, quem cœperant colere. Sicque timuerunt eum nunc timore magno et initiali seu filiali, ita quod pœnitendo et bonum propositum concipiendo, fecerunt quod in ipsis est, moxque gratiam gratum facientem sortiti sunt.
paras.en: [[1:16|And the men feared the Lord exceedingly|Et timuerunt viri timore magno Dominum]]. For it is natural that a man should be afraid on seeing unusual and wonderful things. Hence it is often found in the Gospel that the crowds, on seeing Christ's miracles, were afraid[[Matt 9:8||]][[Mark 4:40||]][[Mark 5:15||]][[Luke 5:26||]][[Luke 7:16||]]. And these men saw many wonders within one hour: namely the rising of a supernatural storm, and its sudden stilling. [[1:16|and sacrificed victims to the Lord|Et immolaverunt hostias Domino]]: either sacrifices of praise and a contrite spirit and devout prayer, or else bodily victims from the goods they had with them; [[1:16|and made vows|et voverunt vota]], that is, they promised to offer more. Indeed, according to Jerome, they vowed never again to depart from God, whom they had begun to worship. And so they now feared Him with a great fear, an initial or filial one [initial fear: the fear of beginners, between servile and filial fear], so that by repenting and forming a good resolve they did what lay in them, and soon received sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*: the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God].

1.title: De mystica explanatione ejusdem capituli primi.
1.title_en: On the mystical explanation of the same first chapter.

paras.t: Jonas in multis tenet figuram Christi, sicut in sequenti patebit capitulo. Unde quæ litteraliter de Jona inducta sunt, de Christo allegorice exponuntur. Jonas autem interpretatur columba, seu dolens. Et per utrumque intelligitur Christus ab omni felle amaritudinis alienus, purus, et simplex: super quem Spiritus Sanctus in specie columbæ descendit. Ipse quoque est de quo cantatur in Psalmo: Ego sum pauper et dolens. Et in Isaia dicitur: Vere dolores nostros ipse portavit; et, Vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras. Itaque, Factum est verbum, id est præceptum, Domini Dei Patris, ad Jonam, id est Christum, secundum quod homo est. Propter quod ait in Joannis evangelio: Sic ut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio. Filium Amathi, id est Patris æterni, qui est veritas prima. Amathi nempe veritas interpretatur.
paras.en: Jonas in many things bears the figure of Christ, as will appear in the following chapter. Hence what has been set down of Jonas according to the letter is expounded allegorically of Christ. Now Jonas is interpreted *dove*, or *sorrowing*. And by both is understood Christ, a stranger to all gall of bitterness, pure and simple: upon whom the Holy Ghost descended in the form of a dove[[Matt 3:16||]]. He it is, too, of whom it is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:30|I am poor and sorrowful|Ego sum pauper et dolens]]. And in Isaias it is said: [[Is 53:4|Surely|Vere]] he hath [[Is 53:4|carried our sorrows|dolores nostros ipse portavit]]; and, [[Is 53:5|he was wounded for our iniquities|Vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras]]. Accordingly, [[1:1|the word|Factum est verbum]] (that is, the command) of the Lord God the Father came to Jonas, that is, to Christ according as He is man. Wherefore He says in John's gospel: [[John 14:31|as the Father hath given me commandments, so do I|Sic ut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio]]. [[1:1|The son of Amathi|Filium Amathi]], that is, of the eternal Father, who is the first truth; for Amathi is interpreted *truth*.

paras.t: Surge a quiete contemplationis, vel, a Nazareth urbe permodica, et vade in Niniven civitatem grandem, id est ad mundum seu populum universum. Ninive autem interpretatur speciosa: qua mundus designatur, quo oculis carnis nil pulchrius intuemur. Unde in Græco ab ornatu seu pulchritudine nomen accepit, quoniam Græce dicitur κόσμος, id est decorus sive ornatus. Hinc etiam Plato disseruit, quod mundus iste sensibilis, dicitur mundus, id est purus, quoniam a mundo mundissimo, qui est in mente divina, videlicet a mundo ideali atque archetypo, fluxit. Et prædica in ea, quia ascendit malitia ejus. Hoc Christus prædicavit, dicendo: Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis; et, Væ mundo a scandalis. Propter quod ait in Joanne: Me odit mundus, quia ego testimonium perhibeo de illo, quia opera ejus mala sunt. Hoc et Isaias prædixit: Percutiet, inquiens, terram virga oris sui.
paras.en: [[1:2|Arise|Surge]] from the quiet of contemplation, or from Nazareth, a very small town, [[1:2|and go to Ninive, the great city|et vade in Niniven civitatem grandem]], that is, to the world, or to the whole people. Now Ninive is interpreted *beautiful*: by which the world is signified, than which we behold nothing more beautiful with the eyes of the flesh. Hence in Greek it took its name from adornment or beauty, since in Greek it is called κόσμος, that is, comely or adorned. Hence too Plato taught that this sensible world is called *mundus*, that is, pure [the Latin *mundus* means both "world" and "clean"], because it flowed from the most pure world which is in the divine mind, namely from the ideal and archetypal world. [[1:2|and preach in it: For the wickedness thereof is come up|Et prædica in ea, quia ascendit malitia ejus]]. This Christ preached, saying: [[Luke 13:5|except you do penance, you shall all likewise perish|Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis]]; and, [[Matt 18:7|Woe to the world because of scandals|Væ mundo a scandalis]]. Wherefore He says in John, of the world: [[John 7:7|me it hateth, because I give testimony of it, that the works thereof are evil|Me odit mundus, quia ego testimonium perhibeo de illo, quia opera ejus mala sunt]]. This Isaias also foretold: [[Is 11:4|he shall strike|Percutiet]], he says, [[Is 11:4|the earth with the rod of his mouth|terram virga oris sui]].

paras.t: Denique in hoc quod Jonas fugit a facie Domini, non tenet proprie typum Christi. Et descendit in Joppen. Per Joppen, quæ interpretatur decora, virgo Maria tota pulchra et penitus immaculata exprimitur, cujus dulcissimum virginalemque uterum ingressus est Filius Dei; et invenit navem, id est, carnem humanam sumpsit ex ea, euntem in Tharsis, id est in mare sæculi hujus. Procedens namque de Virginis utero, processit ad persecutiones mundi istius. Et dedit naulum ejus, id est, corpori assumpto largitus est præmium pro ministerio quo ministravit Verbo æterno, cujus erat instrumentum animatum, conjunctum, immediatum et proprium. Et descendit in eam: divinitas quippe latebat et habitavit in carne assumpta; ut iret in Tharsis, id est, visibiliter conversaretur cum hominibus et prædicaret in mundo.
paras.en: Lastly, in this, that Jonas fled from the face of the Lord, he does not properly bear the type of Christ. [[1:3|And he went down to Joppe|Et descendit in Joppen]]. By Joppe, which is interpreted *comely*, is expressed the Virgin Mary, all fair and wholly immaculate[[Cant 4:7||]], whose most sweet and virginal womb the Son of God entered; [[1:3|and found a ship|et invenit navem]], that is, He took human flesh of her, [[1:3|going to Tharsis|euntem in Tharsis]], that is, into the sea of this world. For coming forth from the Virgin's womb, He went forth to the persecutions of this world. [[1:3|And he paid the fare thereof|Et dedit naulum ejus]], that is, He bestowed on the body He had taken a reward for the service with which it served the eternal Word, whose instrument it was, animate, conjoined, immediate and proper [that is, a living instrument united to the Word directly and belonging to Him alone]. [[1:3|And went down into it|Et descendit in eam]]: for the Godhead lay hidden and dwelt in the flesh assumed; [[1:3|to go|ut iret]] to Tharsis, that is, that He might converse visibly with men[[Bar 3:38||]] and preach in the world.

paras.t: Dominus autem misit ventum magnum in mare, id est, multas persecutiones permisit excitari in Christum; et facta est tempestas magna in mari, id est in Judæa vitiorum fluctibus plena et amarissima, quando videlicet Scribæ ac Pharisæi cum aliis multis persecuti sunt Christum. Unde in Evangelio legitur, quod Christo ingrediente Jerusalem, commota est universa civitas, dicens: Quis est hic? Et navis periclitabatur conteri, secundum exteriorem apparentiam, quando Judæi voluerunt Jesum præcipitare et lapidare. Per navem autem, ut dictum est, intelligitur caro Christi, quæ erat quasi vehiculum deitatis, præsertim quum nobis quoque dicat Apostolus: Portate Deum in corpore vestro. Et alibi scriptum est: Currus Dei decem millibus multiplex. In die vero Parasceves contrita est navis ista, quantum ad hoc quod humanam vitam amisit, et a planta usque ad verticem non erat sanitas in ea.
paras.en: [[1:4|But the Lord sent a great wind to the sea|Dominus autem misit ventum magnum in mare]], that is, He permitted many persecutions to be stirred up against Christ; [[1:4|and a great tempest was raised in the sea|et facta est tempestas magna in mari]], that is, in Judea, full of the waves of vices and most bitter, namely when the Scribes and Pharisees with many others persecuted Christ. Hence we read in the Gospel that when Christ entered Jerusalem, [[Matt 21:10|the whole city was moved, saying: Who is this?|commota est universa civitas, dicens: Quis est hic?]] [[1:4|And the ship was in danger to be broken|Et navis periclitabatur conteri]], according to outward appearance, when the Jews wished to cast Jesus down headlong[[Luke 4:29||]] and to stone Him[[John 8:59||]][[John 10:31||]]. Now by the ship, as has been said, is understood the flesh of Christ, which was as it were the vehicle of the Godhead; all the more since the Apostle says to us too: [[1 Cor 6:20|bear God in your body|Portate Deum in corpore vestro]]. And elsewhere it is written: [[Ps 67:18|The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands|Currus Dei decem millibus multiplex]]. And on the day of the Parasceve [that is, Good Friday, the day of Preparation] this ship was broken, inasmuch as it lost its human life, and [[Is 1:6|from the sole of the foot unto the top of the head, there is no soundness therein|a planta usque ad verticem non erat sanitas in ea]].

paras.t: Quumque comprehensus esset Christus a Judæis, nautæ, id est Apostoli navem Ecclesiæ postea gubernantes, timuerunt, fugientes a Christo, et clamaverunt ad Deum, eo quod dulcissimum atque carissimum amiserunt magistrum.
paras.en: And when Christ had been seized by the Jews, [[1:5|the mariners|nautæ]], that is, the Apostles who afterwards steered the ship of the Church, [[1:5|were afraid|timuerunt]], fleeing from Christ[[Matt 26:56||]], and [[1:5|cried|clamaverunt]] to God, because they had lost their most sweet and most dear master.

paras.t: Et Jonas descendit ad interiora navis, et dormiebat sopore gravi. Sic et Christus dormivit in navi super cervical, secundum Marcum. Et accessit ad eum gubernator. Petrus enim, princeps Apostolorum, et condiscipuli tunc suscitaverunt Jesum.
paras.en: [[1:5|and Jonah went down into the inner part of the ship, and fell into a deep sleep|Et Jonas descendit ad interiora navis, et dormiebat sopore gravi]]. So too Christ slept in the ship [[Mark 4:38|upon a pillow|super cervical]], according to Mark. [[1:6|And the ship master came to him|Et accessit ad eum gubernator]]: for Peter, the prince of the Apostles, and his fellow disciples then awoke Jesus[[Mark 4:38||]].

paras.t: Verumtamen per soporem Jonæ, aptius intelligitur torpor et negligentia peccatoris: qui quum in medio laqueorum ambulet, et infinitis valletur periculis, vana securitate resolvitur, nec cum timore et tremore propriam operatur salutem. Unde in Ecclesiaste habetur: Sunt impii qui ita securi sunt, quasi justorum facta habeant. Tales ergo accedat gubernator, id est prælatus vel pius hortator atque director (unicuique enim mandavit Deus de proximo suo), et dicat: Quid tu sopore deprimeris? Surge, invoca Deum tuum. Ambrosius: Tempus enim est nos a somno surgere, quoniam non dormientibus, pigritantibus, acediosis, sed vigilantibus et laborantibus, provenit regnum cœlorum. Ideo ait Salvator: Vigilate itaque, omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere omnia quæ ventura sunt, et stare ante Filium hominis; et alibi, Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis diem neque horam. Hinc in Proverbiis Salomonis dicitur: Usquequo, piger, dormies? Usquequo dormitabis? Si forte recogitet Deus de nobis, ut non pereamus. Ita in omni tribulatione et angustia facere nos oportet, confugiendo ad Deum, et alios admonendo ut invocent Deum: quia quum ignoramus quid facere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros et corda levemus ad Creatorem.
paras.en: Yet by the sleep of Jonas is more fitly understood the torpor and negligence of the sinner, who, though he walks in the midst of snares and is hemmed in by countless dangers, is slackened by a vain security, and does not work out his own salvation [[Phil 2:12|with fear and trembling|cum timore et tremore]]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:14|there are wicked men, who are as secure as though they had the deeds of the just|Sunt impii qui ita securi sunt, quasi justorum facta habeant]]. To such, then, let the ship master come, that is, the prelate, or a devout exhorter and director (for God [[Ecclus 17:12|gave to every one of them commandment concerning his neighbour|unicuique enim mandavit Deus de proximo suo]]), and let him say: [[1:6|Why art thou fast asleep? rise up call upon thy God|Quid tu sopore deprimeris? Surge, invoca Deum tuum]]. Ambrose: For [[Rom 13:11|it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep|Tempus enim est nos a somno surgere]], since the kingdom of heaven comes not to the sleeping, the slothful and the listless [*acediosis*: those given to acedia, spiritual sloth], but to those who watch and labour. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Luke 21:36|Watch ye, therefore, praying at all times, that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of man|Vigilate itaque, omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere omnia quæ ventura sunt, et stare ante Filium hominis]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 25:13|Watch ye therefore, because you know not the day nor the hour|Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis diem neque horam]]. Hence it is said in the Proverbs of Solomon: [[Prov 6:9|How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?|Usquequo, piger, dormies?]] How long wilt thou slumber? [the second question is not in the Vulgate of Prov 6:9, which goes on: when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Compare Prov 6:10: thou wilt slumber a little] [[1:6|if so be that God will think of us that we may not perish|Si forte recogitet Deus de nobis, ut non pereamus]]. So must we do in every tribulation and distress, fleeing to God and admonishing others to call upon God: because, [[2 Par 20:12|as we know not what to do, we can only turn our eyes|quum ignoramus quid facere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros]], and our hearts, up to the Creator.

paras.t: Dixit Jonas: Tollite me, et mittite in mare. Sic Christus videns totum genus humanum periclitari, et pro magna parte damnari, voluit in hunc mundum descendere, hominesque moriendo salvare a tempestate dæmonis et peccati: præsertim, quoniam Pater zelans pro Filio, damnavit angelicos spiritus protoplastosque homines, eo quod similitudinem Dei, quæ Filio appropriatur vel propria est, inordinate appetierunt. Hinc Filius zelans pro Patre, ut ejus honorem in hominibus recuperaret, dignatus est in mare sæculi destinari et opprimi, prout fatetur in Psalmo: Super me confirmatus est furor tuus, et omnes fluctus tuos induxisti super me. Et cessabit mare a vobis. Christo enim pro nobis occiso, mitigata est rabies dæmonum in nos: non quod illi minus crudeles effecti sint, sed quia eorum potestas arctata est.
paras.en: Jonas [[1:12|said|Dixit]]: [[1:12|take me up, and cast me into the sea|Tollite me, et mittite in mare]]. So Christ, seeing the whole human race in peril and for the most part damned, willed to come down into this world and by dying to save men from the tempest of the devil and of sin: all the more since the Father, jealous for the Son, condemned the angelic spirits and our first parents [*protoplastos*, the first-formed, Adam and Eve], because they inordinately desired the likeness of God, which is appropriated to the Son or is proper to Him. Hence the Son, jealous for the Father, so as to recover His honour among men, deigned to be sent into the sea of the world and to be overwhelmed, as He confesses in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:8|Thy wrath is strong over me: and all thy waves thou hast brought in upon me.|Super me confirmatus est furor tuus, et omnes fluctus tuos induxisti super me]] [[1:12|and the sea shall be calm to you|Et cessabit mare a vobis]]. For when Christ was slain for us, the rage of the demons against us was assuaged: not that they have become less cruel, but because their power has been restrained.

paras.t: Et timuerunt viri timore magno. Sic et nos videntes indesinenter magnalia Dei, rapidum motum cœlorum, cursus stellarum, etc., quæ in universo geruntur a Deo, quæ utique incomparabiliter majora sunt quam quæ viri prædicti viderunt circa Jonam, debemus Deum filialiter revereri, multumque timere, et cordialiter concuti ex consideratione majestatis omnipotentiæ Dei, hostias quoque obedientiæ, laudis ac precum Deo offerre, et vota vovere, juxta illud: Vovete et reddite Domino Deo vestro. Hoc enim est actus latriæ.
paras.en: [[1:16|And the men feared|Et timuerunt viri]] [[1:16|exceedingly|timore magno]]. So we too, who see without ceasing the great works of God, the swift motion of the heavens, the courses of the stars, etc., which are wrought by God in the universe, and which are beyond compare greater than what the aforesaid men saw in the case of Jonas, ought to revere God as sons, and greatly to fear Him, and to be shaken to the heart by the consideration of the majesty of God's omnipotence; and also to offer to God victims of obedience, of praise and of prayer, and to vow vows, according to the word: [[Ps 75:12|Vow ye, and pay to the Lord your God|Vovete et reddite Domino Deo vestro]]. For this is an act of latria [that is, of the worship due to God alone].

2.title: Expositio litteralis capituli secundi: Et præparavit Dominus piscem grandem, etc.
2.title_en: Literal exposition of the second chapter: Now the Lord prepared a great fish, etc.

paras.t: Consequenter describuntur mirabilia Dei circa Jonam peracta. Et præparavit, id est, ad deglutiendum Jonam adduxit, Dominus piscem grandem, id est cetum. Sic enim Christus allegat in Evangelio: Sicut fuit Jonas in ventre ceti, etc. Sic quoque transtulerunt Septuaginta. Ut deglutiret Jonam. Poterat utique Deus conservare vitam Jonæ extra ventrem ceti in pelago; sed ad præfigurandam dominicam sepulturam, voluit eum esse in medio ceti, cujus venter figuravit Christi sepulcrum. Præparavit autem Dominus piscem hunc, vel de novo eum producendo, vel de alio loco ad navem ducendo: quod forte ministerio angeli factum est, quanquam et solo nutu Deus hoc potuit. Et erat Jonas in ventre piscis, vivus atque incolumis potestate divina, sicut tres pueri in medio æstuantis incendii, tribus diebus et tribus noctibus, propter mysterium seu mysticam rationem, ad præfigurandum tri[…]
paras.en: Next are described the wonders that God wrought concerning Jonas. [[2:1|Now the Lord prepared|Et præparavit]], that is, brought up to swallow Jonas, [[2:1|a great fish|Dominus piscem grandem]], that is, a whale. For so Christ cites it in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:40|as Jonas was in the whale's belly|Sicut fuit Jonas in ventre ceti]], etc. So too the Septuagint translated it. [[2:1|to swallow up Jonah|Ut deglutiret Jonam]]. God could certainly have preserved the life of Jonas in the sea outside the whale's belly; but to prefigure the Lord's burial he willed him to be within the whale, whose belly figured the sepulchre of Christ. And the Lord prepared this fish either by producing it anew, or by bringing it from some other place to the ship: which was perhaps done by the ministry of an angel, though God could have done it by his nod alone. [[2:1|and Jonah was in the belly of a fish|Et erat Jonas in ventre piscis]], alive and unharmed by the divine power, as the three children were in the midst of the raging fire[[Dan 3:49||]][[Dan 3:50||]], [[2:1|for three days and three nights|tribus diebus et tribus noctibus]], on account of a mystery or mystical reason, to prefigure the three[…] [the rest of this sentence is missing from the transcribed text; it presumably went on to the Lord's three days in the tomb]

paras.t: Et oravit Jonas ad Dominum Deum suum de ventre piscis, et dixit: Clamavi, vel solo cordis affectu verbisque mentalibus, vel clamore vocali, quia in ventre piscis potuit vox formari, de tribulatione mea, id est, in tribulatione exsistens, et ab ea eripi cupiens, ad Dominum, qui ait: Invoca me in die tribulationis; et exaudivit me de ventre inferi, id est, de utero piscis, qui inferus similitudinarie appellatur, propter horrorem et capacitatis latitudinem. Erat enim perhorrendum, esse in medio ceti. Sic et nos in tribulatione facere opus est, exemplo dicentis: Ad Dominum, quum tribularer, clamavi, et exaudivit me. Hinc in Deuteronomio habetur: Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; si tamen toto corde quæsieris eum, et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ. Et Baruch ait: Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva et infirma, et oculi deficientes, et anima esuriens dat gloriam et justitiam tibi Domino. Clamavi, et exaudisti vocem meam. Clamavit enim Jonas, secundum Hieronymum, saltem interno clamore, quando vidit super se venire atque hiare immanem belluam. Et tunc Dominus misericors fuit ei, ita quod non lædebatur ab ea. Cognovit quoque in spiritu se liberandum, et egressurum de ventre ceti, ut aliqui dicunt.
paras.en: [[2:2|And Jonah prayed to the Lord, his God, out of the belly of the fish|Et oravit Jonas ad Dominum Deum suum de ventre piscis]]. [[2:3|And he said: I cried|et dixit: Clamavi]], either by the mere affection of the heart and with words of the mind, or with a cry of the voice, since a voice could be formed in the belly of the fish, [[2:3|out of my affliction|de tribulatione mea]], that is, being in tribulation and longing to be snatched out of it, [[2:3|to the Lord|ad Dominum]], who says: [[Ps 49:15|call upon me in the day of trouble|Invoca me in die tribulationis]]; [[2:3|and he heard me|et exaudivit me]] [[2:3|out of the belly of hell|de ventre inferi]], that is, out of the womb of the fish, which is called hell by a likeness, because of its horror and the breadth of its capacity. For it was a most dreadful thing to be within a whale. So we too must do in tribulation, after the example of him who says: [[Ps 119:1|In my trouble I cried to the Lord: and he heard me|Ad Dominum, quum tribularer, clamavi, et exaudivit me]]. Hence it is said in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 4:29|when thou shalt seek there the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him: yet so, if thou seek him with all thy heart, and all the affliction of thy soul|Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; si tamen toto corde quæsieris eum, et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ]]. And Baruch says: [[Bar 2:18|the soul that is sorrowful for the greatness of evil she hath done, and goeth bowed down, and feeble, and the eyes that fail, and the hungry soul giveth glory and justice to thee the Lord|Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva et infirma, et oculi deficientes, et anima esuriens dat gloriam et justitiam tibi Domino]]. [[2:3|I cried|Clamavi]], [[2:3|and thou hast heard my voice|et exaudisti vocem meam]]. For Jonas cried, according to Jerome, at least with an inward cry, when he saw the huge beast coming upon him and gaping. And then the Lord was merciful to him, so that he was not hurt by it. He knew also in spirit that he would be set free and would come out of the whale's belly, as some say.

paras.t: Et projecisti me in profundum in corde maris, id est in cetum, qui quum sit maximæ quantitatis inter pisces, descendit ad profundiora pelagi loca, ut posset natare. Hoc loco dicit Hieronymus, quod infernus esse perhibetur in medio terræ. Et flumen circumdedit me, id est fluens aqua abyssi, antequam glutiretur; et etiam in ventre ceti fuit aqua Jonam circumdans pro aliqua corporis sui parte. Omnes gurgites tui et fluctus tui a te creati et mihi inflicti, super me transierunt. Operuerunt enim piscem, et ex consequenti eum qui fuit in medio piscis.
paras.en: [[2:4|And thou hast cast me forth into the deep, in the heart of the sea|Et projecisti me in profundum in corde maris]], that is, into the whale, which, being the largest of the fishes, goes down to the deeper places of the sea so that it can swim. At this place Jerome says that hell is held to be in the middle of the earth. [[2:4|and a flood hast compassed me|Et flumen circumdedit me]], that is, the flowing water of the deep, before he was swallowed; and in the whale's belly too there was water surrounding Jonas about some part of his body. [[2:4|all thy billows, and thy waves|Omnes gurgites tui et fluctus tui]], created by thee and laid upon me, [[2:4|have passed over me|super me transierunt]]. For they covered the fish, and in consequence him who was within the fish.

paras.t: Et ego dixi: Abjectus sum a conspectu oculorum tuorum, id est ab intuitu miserationis pietatisque tuæ. Hoc dixit dolentis affectu: et quantum ad hoc, verum fuit quod Deus rigorose coepit inobedientiam ejus punire per tempestatem, projectionem, et deglutitionem. Verumtamen rursus videbo templum sanctum tuum: quia (ut tactum est) spiritu prophetali prævidit se exiturum de pisce, et templum Dei in Jerusalem conspecturum, de quo fertur in Psalmo: Sanctum est templum tuum, mirabile in æquitate.
paras.en: [[2:5|And I said: I am cast away out of the sight of thy eyes|Et ego dixi: Abjectus sum a conspectu oculorum tuorum]], that is, from the gaze of thy compassion and loving-kindness. This he said with the feeling of one in sorrow; and in this respect it was true that God had begun to punish his disobedience severely, by the storm, by his being thrown overboard, and by his being swallowed. [[2:5|but yet I shall see the holy temple again|Verumtamen rursus videbo templum sanctum tuum]]: because (as was touched on above) he foresaw by the prophetic spirit that he would come out of the fish and behold the temple of God in Jerusalem, of which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 64:5|holy is thy temple|Sanctum est templum tuum]], [[Ps 64:6|wonderful in justice|mirabile in æquitate]].

paras.t: Circumdederunt me aquæ usque ad animam meam, id est, usque ad vitæ periculum, nisi divinitus præservatus fuissem. Substantiam vero animæ incorporalem ac simplicem aquæ non possunt contingere vel intrare. Abyssus vallavit me, pelagus operuit caput meum, operiendo piscem in quo eram conclusus, et antequam glutirer.
paras.en: [[2:6|The waters compassed me about even to the soul|Circumdederunt me aquæ usque ad animam meam]], that is, even to the peril of my life, had I not been preserved by God. But the waters cannot touch or enter the substance of the soul, which is incorporeal and simple. [[2:6|the deep hath closed me round about|Abyssus vallavit me]], [[2:6|the sea hath covered my head|pelagus operuit caput meum]], by covering the fish in which I was shut up, and before I was swallowed.

paras.t: Ad extrema montium, id est ad profunda loca abyssi, ubi montium fundamenta, radices seu pedes terminantur (quod accipi potest de magnis montibus in littore vel in mari locatis), descendi; terræ vectes, id est bassiora loca terræ super quam currit abyssus, quibus quasi vectibus et columnis globus terræ dicitur sustentari, vel, profunda terrarum tanquam vectes et serræ, concluserunt me in æternum, secundum hominum æstimationem, vel quia humana virtute nunquam egredi potui: quamvis nullum corpus humanum sit æternaliter permansurum in pelago, sed in die novissimo suscitandum, quando mare dabit mortuos suos, secundum Joannem in Apocalypsi. Et sublevabis, id est eripies, de corruptione, id est morte et digestione seu manducatione a bellua ista, vitam meam, ne manducer a ceto, Domine Deus meus: qui licet sis omnium Deus, tamen specialiter es Deus meus, circa quem tam pie ac mirabiliter operaris.
paras.en: [[2:7|to the lowest parts of the mountains|Ad extrema montium]], that is, to the deep places of the abyss, where the foundations, roots or feet of the mountains end (which can be taken of great mountains set on the shore or in the sea), [[2:7|I went down|descendi]]; [[2:7|the bars of the earth|terræ vectes]], that is, the lower places of the earth over which the deep runs, on which, as on bars and pillars, the globe of the earth is said to be held up; or, the depths of the lands, as bars and bolts [reading *seræ*, "bolts", for the printed *serræ*, "saws"], [[2:7|have shut me up for ever|concluserunt me in æternum]], as men would reckon it, or because by human power I could never have got out: although no human body is to remain for ever in the sea, but is to be raised on the last day, when the sea shall give up its dead, according to John in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 20:13||]]. [[2:7|and thou wilt bring up|Et sublevabis]], that is, wilt snatch out, [[2:7|from corruption|de corruptione]], that is, from death and from digestion or devouring by this beast, [[2:7|my life|vitam meam]], lest I be devoured by the whale, [[2:7|O Lord, my God|Domine Deus meus]]: who, though thou art the God of all, art yet in a special way my God, towards whom thou workest so lovingly and so wonderfully.

paras.t: Quum angustiaretur in me anima mea, id est, omni humano esset solatio destituta, et in horrido tenebrosoque ceti alvo consisterem, Domini recordatus sum, ejus misericordiam implorando, qui ait: Cum ipso sum in tribulatione; ut veniat ad te, Domine, oratio mea, id est, tibi accepta sit, ad templum sanctum tuum, id est ad te in templo tuo specialiter habitantem. Dominus enim in templo sancto suo: sive per templum intelligatur quod erat in Jerusalem, sive templum triumphantis Ecclesiæ, quod est patria cœlestis, vel cœlum empyreum. Quod autem in Apocalypsi habetur, Templum non vidi in ea, intelligitur quantum ad aliquem actum templi, qui convenit viatoribus, non comprehensoribus.
paras.en: [[2:8|When my soul was in distress within me|Quum angustiaretur in me anima mea]], that is, was bereft of all human comfort, and I lay in the horrid and dark belly of the whale, [[2:8|I remembered the Lord|Domini recordatus sum]], imploring the mercy of him who says: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation|Cum ipso sum in tribulatione]]; [[2:8|that my prayer may come to thee|ut veniat ad te, Domine, oratio mea]], O Lord, that is, may be acceptable to thee, [[2:8|unto the holy temple|ad templum sanctum tuum]], that is, to thee who dwellest in a special way in thy temple. For [[Ps 10:5|The Lord is in his holy temple|Dominus enim in templo sancto suo]]: whether by the temple be understood that which was in Jerusalem, or the temple of the Church triumphant, which is the heavenly fatherland, or the empyrean heaven. And what is said in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 21:22|I saw no temple therein|Templum non vidi in ea]], is understood with regard to some act of the temple which befits wayfarers, not those who have attained [that is, *viatores*, those still on the way in this life, as against *comprehensores*, the blessed who have reached God].

paras.t: Qui custodiunt vanitates, id est, rebus vanis, mendaciis et peccatis diligenter inhærent, et velut carum thesaurum conservant, lætantes quum malefecerint, et perseverantes in malis, frustra misericordiam suam derelinquunt, id est, gratia et misericordia Dei se indignos inaniter faciunt, quia nec in illis aliquid veræ beatitudinis reperiunt, et veram felicitatem amittunt. Et in hoc patet magnanimitas Jonæ, quod in tanto constitutus horrore, contra mundanam prosperitatem invehitur.
paras.en: They that [[2:9|observe vanities|custodiunt vanitates]], that is, cling diligently to vain things, to lies and sins, and keep them like a precious treasure, being [[Prov 2:14|glad when they have done evil|lætantes quum malefecerint]], and persevering in evil, [[2:9|in vain|frustra]] [[2:9|forsake their own mercy|misericordiam suam derelinquunt]] [Denis takes *frustra*, "in vain", with what follows], that is, to no purpose make themselves unworthy of the grace and mercy of God, since in those things they find nothing of true beatitude, and they lose true happiness. And in this the greatness of soul of Jonas is plain, that, set in so great a horror, he inveighs against worldly prosperity.

paras.t: Ego autem in voce laudis, id est cum cantico et divino præconio, immolabo tibi hostias spirituales atque legales, et in primis me ipsum, tibi de cetero in omnibus obediendo. Salutare enim sacrificium est, attendere in mandatis, et discedere ab omni iniquitate, ut dicitur in Ecclesiastico. Quæcumque vovi, reddam. Unde patet, quod Jonas more afflictorum promisit certas Deo hostias immolare, vel obsequia exhibere, vel pro gratiarum actione, quod Deus eum tam clementer custodivit in mari, vel ut tantum discrimen evaderet, nec fieret belluæ cibus. Pro salute mea Domino, ut ab eo æternam merear beatitudinem consequi.
paras.en: [[2:10|But I with the voice of praise|Ego autem in voce laudis]], that is, with song and the proclaiming of God's praise, [[2:10|will sacrifice to thee|immolabo tibi]] victims spiritual and legal [that is, both the inward offerings of the soul and the sacrifices prescribed by the Law], and first of all myself, obeying thee henceforth in all things. For [[Ecclus 35:2|It is a wholesome sacrifice to take heed to the commandments, and to depart from all iniquity|Salutare enim sacrificium est, attendere in mandatis, et discedere ab omni iniquitate]], as is said in Ecclesiasticus. [[2:10|I will pay whatsoever I have vowed|Quæcumque vovi, reddam]]. Hence it is plain that Jonas, as the afflicted do, promised to offer God certain victims or to render him certain services, either in thanksgiving, because God had kept him so mercifully in the sea, or so that he might escape so great a peril and not become food for the beast. [[2:10|for my salvation to the Lord|Pro salute mea Domino]], that I may deserve to obtain eternal beatitude from him.

paras.t: Et dixit, id est, jussit, Dominus, cui cuncta creata obediunt, pisci, movendo et afficiendo appetitum piscis ad id quod subditur; et evomuit Jonam in aridam, projiciendo eum super littus maris. Et miraculosum videtur fuisse, quod tantus piscis potuit terræ eatenus propinquare, quia in modica aqua natare non valet. Potest tamen cum impetu venire ad littus, deferendo ante se aquam, sicut dum capitur; sed si tunc aliquid extra se projicit, hoc cadit in aquam.
paras.en: [[2:11|And the Lord spoke|Et dixit]] (that is, gave command: the Lord, whom all created things obey) [[2:11|to the fish|pisci]], moving and stirring the fish's appetite to what follows; [[2:11|and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land|et evomuit Jonam in aridam]], casting him up on the seashore. And it seems to have been a miracle that so great a fish could come so near the land, since it cannot swim in shallow water. Yet it can come with a rush to the shore, driving the water before it, as when it is being caught; but if it then casts anything out of itself, this falls into the water.

paras.t: Præterea, juxta allegoricum intellectum, quemadmodum Jonæ triduana in pisce habitatio, fuit sepulturæ dominicæ typus, sic ejus oratio fuit figura orationis Domini Salvatoris, qui secundum Apostolum, cum clamore valido et lacrimis supplicationes fudit ad Deum. Clamavi de tribulatione mea ad Dominum. Sic et Christus passione instante precatus est: Pater, si fieri potest, transeat a me calix iste. Et in cruce extentus: Deus, Deus meus, respice in me. Et exaudivit me de ventre inferi, id est, de limbo animam meam eduxit, et corpori reunivit; vel, De ventre inferi, id est de monumento. Clamavi, et exaudisti vocem meam: juxta quod ait in Joanne: Pater, gratias ago tibi, quoniam audisti me; ego autem sciebam quoniam semper me audis. Quidquid enim Christus oravit ratione deliberata et voluntate rationali simpliciter dicta, obtinuit.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the allegorical sense: as Jonas's three days' dwelling in the fish was a type of the Lord's burial, so his prayer was a figure of the prayer of the Lord our Saviour, who, according to the Apostle, poured forth supplications to God [[Heb 5:7|with a strong cry and tears|cum clamore valido et lacrimis]]. [[2:3|I cried out of my affliction to the Lord|Clamavi de tribulatione mea ad Dominum]]. So Christ too prayed when his passion was at hand: [[Matt 26:39|Father, if it be possible|Pater, si fieri potest]], [[Matt 26:39|let this chalice pass from me|transeat a me calix iste]]. And when stretched out on the cross: [[Ps 21:2|O God my God, look upon me|Deus, Deus meus, respice in me]]. [[2:3|and he heard me|Et exaudivit me]] [[2:3|out of the belly of hell|de ventre inferi]], that is, he brought my soul out of limbo and united it again to the body; or, [[2:3|out of the belly of hell|De ventre inferi]], that is, out of the tomb. [[2:3|I cried|Clamavi]], [[2:3|and thou hast heard my voice|et exaudisti vocem meam]]: according to what he says in John: [[John 11:41|Father, I give thee thanks that thou hast heard me|Pater, gratias ago tibi, quoniam audisti me]]; [[John 11:42|And I knew that thou hearest me always|ego autem sciebam quoniam semper me audis]].
